Intent: Introduce characters and the first spark of connection: Elinor slips into the walled garden to escape the day's talk of alliances and meets Thomas, who returns her lost locket. Establish their differing worlds, the locket as token, Mara's cautious sympathy, and the manor's rigid separations.
Present: char-elinor-ashbury, char-thomas-brennan, char-mara-sibyl, loc-ashbury-garden, obj-elinor-locket, loc-ashbury-manor, obj-thomas-handkerchief
The P0 and P1 material is already assembled and is below. You cannot change it.
Your job is what it does not know to look for: something established long ago that
this scene touches, a promise falling due, a place or object that has been described
before, a relationship whose history matters here.
Search the index with the shell, and **batch it**. One command can answer several
questions, and one reply can carry several tool calls — measured, you averaged 22.5
round-trips per build with 96% of them carrying a single read, each re-sending a
transcript that had grown to 12,000 tokens to get one file back. That loop is most of
what a run spends and most of how long it takes.
So decide what you want, then ask for it all at once. `read_index` takes a **list** of
paths — one call for ten files costs one round-trip, ten calls cost ten:
  read_index paths=["characters/char-a/profile.yaml", "objects/obj-key.yaml", …]
  grep -rn "<id-a>\|<id-b>\|<id-c>" novel/chapters/ | tail -40
  cat characters/*/state.jsonl continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl relations/<a>--<b>.yaml
  ls relations/ objects/ locations/
A second round-trip is worth it when what you read next depends on what came back. It
is not worth it for a list of files you had already chosen.
Scenes written so far: s-001.
This scene is in the opening third. There is little behind it, so recall is cheap and mostly unnecessary — check the scene before it and the entity files, and do not pad. An item added here is an item the writer and the verifier both read.
Add what you find with add_context_item. Quote the material; a pointer is not context.
Add nothing if there is nothing — a padded packet costs the writer attention it needs
for the scene, and every item you add is also an item the verifier reads.
Then record what you could **not** find, with note_gap. Read the scene's intent and ask
what a writer must know to write it: what this place looks like, whether these two have
met, what exactly was promised. For each one you searched for and did not find, note it.
This half matters as much as the first. What you add, the writer uses; what you record
as missing is what the writer would otherwise invent without noticing it was inventing —
and an invented fact is indistinguishable from an established one the moment it is on
the page.

Everything you add is assembled into .context-builder/history/ch-01/s-001.md, which is the document the writer works from. If it asks a follow-up later, your answer is appended to that same file rather than sent as a loose reply — so answer as though you were adding to the packet, because you are.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Scene s-001 (ch-01): Introduce Elinor, Thomas and Mara in the walled garden and establish the first spark between Elinor and Thomas. The writer will need concrete sensory details of the garden and the manor's separation (sightlines, servants' paths), the physical description and small gestures that show class difference without caricature, and the provenance of obj-elinor-locket (how lost/found) and obj-thomas-handkerchief (how it is carried/repaired). Do not invent any new entities. Emphasize restraint and quiet tenderness: a scene of small exchanged tokens (the locket returned) and tentative, charged conversation. Scene length target ~875 words; mark any gaps discovered (e.g., exact time of day, weather) so the writer can ask up to 2 follow-up questions. Note: this is opening scene; keep stakes intimate but hint at Lord Ashbury's pressure (voices from the manor or servants talking of Sir Edmund) without having Lord Ashbury present.

That is in addition to the above, not instead of it.
Finish by saying in one sentence what you added and which files you read it from.

Scene s-001. Intent: Introduce characters and the first spark of connection: Elinor slips into the walled garden to escape the day's talk of alliances and meets Thomas, who returns her lost locket. Establish their differing worlds, the locket as token, Mara's cautious sympathy, and the manor's rigid separations.

Target length: about 875 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

A sheltered lord's daughter and a lowly servant forge a secret tenderness that the strict hierarchy and a father's sense of honour cannot contain; when a misplaced token and a devoted steward conspire against them, the lovers’ choice to defy rank ends in a private, irreversible tragedy.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-elinor-ashbury: The lord's only daughter, nineteen; raised in genteel confinement, spirited and quietly rebellious, with a secret tenderness for the natural world and a habit of carrying a small silver locket.
- char-lord-ashbury: The proud, conservative lord of Ashbury manor in his late forties; a man of rigid honour and reputation who measures family, land and alliances above personal feeling.
- char-thomas-brennan: A twenty-five-year-old servant who works outside and in the kitchens; steady, literate beyond most servants, taciturn, and unexpectedly tender — he keeps a simple silk handkerchief he once mended for Elinor.
- char-gavin-hale: The steward of the household; dutiful, watchful, and loyal to Lord Ashbury's order. He knows the workings of the manor and notices small irregularities others miss.
- char-mara-sibyl: Elinor's childhood attendant and the head housemaid; sympathetic to Elinor and practical. She is the bridge between the girl's world and the servants' world and sometimes passes messages incautiously.
- char-sir-edmund-harrow: A neighbouring baronet and the suitor Lord Ashbury has chosen for Elinor; prosperous and well-mannered, he embodies the safe, political marriage her father wants.
- char-father-bennet: The parish priest, who presides over ceremonies and counsels the household on conscience and custom; a man who prefers order but feels compassion when confronted with human pain.
- loc-ashbury-manor: The great house of Ashbury: stone halls, low-ceilinged family rooms, staff quarters below, and a walled garden to the north; its architecture enforces social separation.
- loc-ashbury-garden: A cultivated walled garden with a path by a small fountain and fruit trees; where Elinor slips away to breathe and where she and Thomas first have a private conversation.
- loc-kitchen: A warm, bustling space below stairs where servants live some of their truth; its narrow ledges and hidden corners provide opportunities for secret exchanges.
- loc-tower-chamber: Elinor's secluded small chamber on the manor's tower — a high window, a narrow bed, and a view of the estate; where she keeps the locket and tries to hide her feelings.
- loc-chapel: A small private chapel within the manor, used for family worship and formalities like betrothals; a place where community, ceremony and confession intersect.
- obj-elinor-locket: A small silver locket engraved with the Ashbury knot; Elinor's most private possession and a token she shares symbolically with Thomas.
- obj-thomas-handkerchief: A simple silk handkerchief Thomas carries; he once washed and mended it for Elinor — later it will become a fragile proof of intimacy.
- obj-lord-signet: Lord Ashbury's signet ring, used to seal family orders and letters; a symbol of authority whose presence and use determine fates in the household.
- obj-waxed-letter: A sealed letter (blank now) whose discovery or misdelivery will be used as evidence and misinterpreted in the story's turning point.
- obj-poison-phial: A small phial of a herbal draught kept in the apothecary chest; not magical — an instrument of tragic choice if the scene requires it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural or anachronistic elements: all events must be realistic and historically plausible within a late-feudal/early-modern aristocratic household.
- Class and legal rules constrain marriage: a servant cannot lawfully marry the lord's daughter without the lord's explicit consent; betrothal sealed by the lord and priest is socially and legally binding within the story's community.
- The lord's signet and a waxed seal constitute admissible proof of household orders and letters; misdelivery or tampering with sealed correspondence can be interpreted as evidence by household authorities.
- Servants have limited access to private family spaces; evidence of impropriety (tokens in private quarters, misdelivered family letters) is treated as a serious offence and triggers formal inquiry.
- Poisons and draughts exist as ordinary, non-magical substances with lethal potential; their use has realistic physical consequences and legal/moral implications in the story.
